questions.stem: A 35-year-old man attended for care. He was known to have HIV , HCV , and HBV infection related to previous intravenous drug use. He had previously been inconsistent in care but had completed a treatment program for his drug dependency 6 months and now attended regularly for follow up. Investigations: ALT 330 IU/L CD4 430 cells/μL HIV viral load: 90,000 copies/mL; no resistance on genotypic testing HBV sAg positive, eAg positive, cAb positive; HBV eAb negative HBV DNA: 22,000 IU/mL HCV IgG positive, genotype 1; HCV viral load 600,000 IU/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir In a patient co-infected with HBV and HIV , treatment should include tenofovir to cover both viruses. Only A and E include fully active antiretroviral regimens, and only E includes tenofovir. Although lamivudine has activity against HBV , resistance develops quickly. Regimen B would be unconventional and would cover HIV but has no HBV coverage, and ledipasvir alone will not treat HCV . Regimen D includes a single drug for HBV , HIV , and HCV . Both HIV and HCV require more than one active antiviral for efficacy. Given the risk of HBV reactivation with treatment of HCV , in the setting of all three infections, most would recommend controlling HIV and HBV first before starting HCV therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q20

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was being treated for hepatitis C with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir. Investigations: HAV IgG positive HBV cAb positive, HBV sAg negative, HBV sAb 0 HBV DNA undetectable A B HCV IgG positive, HCV genotype 1a Liver biopsy showed grade 1 inflammation and stage 3 fibrosis with features of both chronic HCV and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Baseline Week 4 Week 11 ALT (IU/L) 170 35 2250 AST (IU/L) 289 32 2970 HCV viral load (IU/mL) 1,200,000 Undetectable Undetectable INR 1.8 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 7.2
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely reason for the worsening transaminases?
questions.explanation: Reactivation of HBV Reactivation of HBV in a patient with co-infection with HBV and HCV has been reported in patients being treated for HCV . A patient responding to HCV treatment who has a flare of hepatitis, but still with undetectable HCV viral loads, should be evaluated for HBV . Drug reaction is possible but rarely causes transaminases this elevated. For more information, see https://www.hhs.gov/hepatitis/blog/2017/1/17/hbv-reactivation-during-hcv-treatmen t.html

questions.model_answer: (1) Spontaneous clearance of a past acute HCV infection (resolved infection) with persisting antibody but no viremia. (2) Prior successful treatment with sustained virologic response (cure) - antibody remains detectable. (3) False-positive anti-HCV antibody (low pre-test probability, cross-reactivity); confirm with a second assay. (4) Intermittent or low-level viremia below the assay limit of detection (or very early infection before RNA rises) - repeat HCV RNA.

questions.model_answer: a) Sofosbuvir/ledipasvir: 12 weeks; ribavirin not required for compensated cirrhosis (add ribavirin only if decompensated); interaction - ledipasvir raises tenofovir (TDF) levels (monitor renal function) and ledipasvir absorption is reduced by proton-pump inhibitors; SVR >=97%. b) Sofosbuvir/simeprevir: ~12 weeks but no longer a recommended regimen (pill burden, interactions); efavirenz is a CYP3A4 inducer that lowers simeprevir levels, so co-administration with Atripla is not advised; not for decompensated disease. c) Dasabuvir/ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir (PrOD): genotype 1, ~12 weeks; efavirenz (CYP3A4 inducer) reduces paritaprevir concentrations and the ritonavir booster interacts with the ARV regimen, so it is not recommended with Atripla, and it is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis. d) For sofosbuvir/simeprevir in genotype 1a, test for the Q80K NS3 polymorphism at baseline - its presence substantially reduces simeprevir efficacy.

cohort_answer.text: Labs: Viral load; genotype. Pretreatment evaluation should include risk factors for viral acquisition, signs/symptoms of advanced liver disease or extrahepatic manifestations, cofactors accelerating disease progression (alcohol, obesity, coinfections). Necessary labs: HCV RNA viral load, HCV genotype, liver biochemistry and function, abdominal ultrasound, fibrosis stage assessment, and tests to rule out HBV and HIV coinfection. || Genotype 1a most likely. Genotype 1 infection is the most prevalent genotype in Canada (65% of infected individuals: 56% genotype 1a, 33% genotype 1b, 10% unspecified/mixed). Genotypes 2 and 3 account for ~14% and 20% respectively; genotypes 4, 5, 6 very rare (<1%). (Myers et al., Canadian Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2015) || Interferon-free regimens: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Maviret) x 8 weeks; Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni) x 12 weeks; Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa) x 12 weeks. (Buvir = NS5B polymerase inhibitor; Asvir = NS5A replication complex inhibitor; Previr = NS3 protease inhibitor)

questions.model_answer: a) Ledipasvir-sofosbuvir (Harvoni): 12 weeks in compensated cirrhosis; no ribavirin required; ledipasvir absorption falls with proton-pump inhibitors, and tenofovir levels rise (renal monitoring), while efavirenz lowers ledipasvir exposure. Simeprevir + sofosbuvir: 12 weeks (add ribavirin/consider longer with cirrhosis); efavirenz markedly lowers simeprevir levels, so co-administration is not recommended. Ombitasvir/paritaprevir/dasabuvir + ritonavir: 12 weeks with ribavirin in genotype 1a; the ritonavir-boosted regimen has extensive CYP-mediated interactions and efavirenz is contraindicated with it. b) Test for the NS3 Q80K polymorphism, which confers low-level resistance to simeprevir and reduces response, especially in cirrhosis.

questions.model_answer: a) Two pangenotypic regimens: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir and glecaprevir-pibrentasvir (the triple sofosbuvir-velpatasvir-voxilaprevir is also pangenotypic, used for salvage). b) Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir: sofosbuvir is an NS5B nucleotide polymerase inhibitor, a chain-terminator prodrug incorporated into the growing RNA chain; velpatasvir is an NS5A inhibitor that blocks the NS5A phosphoprotein required for RNA replication and virion assembly. c) In decompensated cirrhosis all NS3/4A protease inhibitors (including glecaprevir) are contraindicated, so choose sofosbuvir-velpatasvir, adding weight-based ribavirin.

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: Epclusa (Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir); Maviret (Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir); Vosevi (Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir/Voxilaprevir) - direct acting antiviral, failures only. Mechanisms - Epclusa: Sofosbuvir - uridine nucleoside inhibitor of HCV NS5B Polymerase (directly acting antiviral), prodrug metabolized to uridine nucleoside triphosphate, chain termination; Velpatasvir - NS5A inhibitor (binds to NS5A protein, blocks ability to regulate replication through unclear mechanism). Maviret: Glecaprevir - Protease inhibitor; Pibrentasvir - NS5A inhibitor. Vosevi: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (see Epclusa); Voxilaprevir - Protease inhibitor. Decompensated cirrhosis: All protease inhibitors are contraindicated so would choose Epclusa plus ribavirin; if MELD >15-18 patient may benefit from deferral of therapy

questions.model_answer: a) Approximately 5-6% (pooled ~5.8%) from HCV-viremic mothers without HIV, rising to roughly 10-11% with HIV co-infection, particularly if the HIV is not virologically suppressed. Transmission is essentially confined to women with detectable HCV RNA.
questions.beyond_mandell: Not in this chapter (Mandell ch. 127 covers HIV MTCT only); figures from AASLD/IDSA HCV guidance and systematic-review data on HCV vertical transmission.

cohort_answer.text: Recent systematic review demonstrated a vertical transmission rate of 5.8% (95% CI 4.2-7.8) from HCV-infected mothers without HIV co-infection, and 10.8% (95% CI 7.6-15.2) with sub-optimally controlled HIV co-infection. ~10% in mothers with HIV and Hep C co-infection; 5-6% in mothers with Hep C mono-infection

parts.text: Four modes of transmission/acquisition.
List four factors affecting response to treatment and prognosis.

parts_raw.text: A) 4 modes of transmission/acquisition
B) List 4 factors affecting response to treatment and prognosis

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Percutaneous exposure to blood via injection drug use; (2) transfusion of blood or blood products (historically, before donor screening); (3) sexual transmission (uncommon except among HIV-positive MSM with high-risk practices); (4) maternal-infant (perinatal) transmission. b) (1) HCV genotype (genotype 3 is the standout for lower response); (2) presence and severity of cirrhosis, particularly decompensated cirrhosis; (3) prior treatment experience, especially prior DAA/NS5A failure; (4) presence of resistance-associated substitutions, primarily NS5A RASs (baseline HCV RNA and HIV co-infection are additional factors).

questions.question: A woman with HCV and HIV co-infection at 18 weeks gestation.
questions.question_raw: HCV and HIV at 18 weeks gestation

parts.text: Risk of transmission of HCV?
Is it necessary to quantify the HCV viral load (PCR) at this point?
Is it safe to breastfeed?
How should the mother deliver the baby?
How should the baby be tested and followed for HCV?

parts_raw.text: Risk of transmission of HCV?
Need to quantify viral load (PCR) at this point?
Safe to breastfeed?
How should the mother deliver the baby
How should the baby be tested and followed for HCV?

questions.model_answer: a) Perinatal HCV transmission is 0-4% with monoinfection but roughly doubles (about 10-11%) with HIV co-infection, and rises further with high maternal viremia. b) No HCV RNA quantification is required for HCV management in pregnancy, as there is no approved intervention to prevent HCV vertical transmission; HIV viral load should be quantified and suppressed. c) Breastfeeding is considered safe with respect to HCV (avoid if nipples are cracked or bleeding), but is contraindicated for HIV in a resource-rich setting. d) HCV alone does not dictate mode of delivery (avoid prolonged rupture of membranes and invasive fetal monitoring); cesarean is recommended for the HIV component if the HIV viral load is >1000 copies/mL or unknown. e) Test the infant with anti-HCV antibody at 18 months (after maternal antibody clears), or HCV RNA PCR on two occasions from 2 months of age if earlier answer is needed; if confirmed positive, refer for genotype and further evaluation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Co-infection transmission figures, viral-load, breastfeeding, delivery, and infant follow-up recommendations are from AASLD-IDSA/CPS and HIV perinatal guidelines; Mandell supports only the monoinfection transmission range.

cohort_answer.text: A) HCV monoinfection: 5-6%; HCV+HIV Coinfection: 10-11%. Risk factors for vertical transmission of HCV: HIV co-infection, viremia, peripheral blood mononuclear cell infection, maternal IVDU. Not risk factors: genotype, breastfeeding, mode of delivery. B) Not needed for Hep C - no safety/efficacy data for treatment to prevent MTCT. Viral load rises during 3rd trimester and drops post-partum, some moms may even clear HCV postpartum. Manage HIV (including quantifying VL and treating). C) Yes for HCV, not safe for HIV, unless nipples cracked/bleeding. D) Any mode of delivery is fine for HCV; avoid obstetrical/fetal procedures, avoid prolonged ROM. C/S preferred for HIV if VL>1000 or unknown at time of delivery. E) HCV serology at 12-18 months (maternal antibodies should have cleared by now). If negative: no follow up needed. If positive: check HCV RNA - if negative: falsely positive antibody; if positive: infected. If significant parental anxiety can do PCR testing at 2 months (no earlier, not sensitive) with serologic follow up as above. If baby confirmed HCV+: genotype, check HBV, HIV, LFTs. Treatment: Age>12y: Genotype 1,4,5,6 - Harvoni (Ledipasvir-sofosbuvir) 12 weeks (24 weeks if cirrhosis); Genotype 2,3 - Epclusa (velpatasvir-sofosbuvir) vs sofosbuvir+RBV; all genotypes - glecaprevir-pibrentasvir 8 weeks, with cirrhosis 12 weeks. Age<12y: wait till 12y, referral to center with expertise in pediatric Hep C, treat once drugs available with approval in this age group.

parts_raw.text: A. What are 2 labs to help you manage this patient?
B. What is the most likely genotype?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) HCV genotype/subtype; (2) quantitative HCV RNA (viral load) — plus assessment of cirrhosis/fibrosis (e.g., elastography) to select regimen and duration. b) Genotype 1, most commonly subtype 1a, in North America. c) Three interferon-free (all-oral DAA) regimens: glecaprevir-pibrentasvir, ledipasvir-sofosbuvir, and sofosbuvir-velpatasvir.
questions.beyond_mandell: The North American predominance of genotype 1a is regional epidemiology not detailed in this chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Liver enzymes, HCV viral load. Genotype. Liver imaging - (eg: fibroscan, ultrasound)

B: HCV 1a. HCV 1a more common than 1b. HCV-1 = 49.1% globally, MOST COMMON - 74.5% in North America. Note: 1a > 1b. HCV-2 = 11% globally, MC in Africa and Asia. HCV-3 = 17.9% globally, MC in Australia, Europe, and Asia. HCV-4 = 16.8% of global HCV infections, MC in central sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa and the Middle East. HCV-5 = MC in east and southern sub-Saharan Africa. HCV-6 = MC in Southeast Asia

C: Fixed-dose glecaprevir 300 mg/pibrentasvir (Maviret) 120 mg once daily for 8 weeks. Fixed-dose ledipasvir 90 mg/sofosbuvir 400 mg (HARVONI) once daily for 12 weeks (reduce to 8 weeks in patients not African American, not HIV-infected, HCV RNA < 6 million IU/mL). Fixed-dose sofosbuvir 400 mg/velpatasvir 100 mg (EPCLUSA) once daily for 12 weeks

questions.question: A patient with compensated cirrhosis and genotype 1a hepatitis C needs treatment. He has HIV on tenofovir/emtricitabine (Truvada) and efavirenz.
questions.question_raw:
Q21 (2015)
Patient with compensated cirrhosis, Genotype 1a Hep C. Needs treatment. Has HIV on truvada/efavirenz.

parts.text: What viral test is needed if the patient is to start simeprevir/sofosbuvir?

parts_raw.text: Last question - what is viral test needed if patient to start simeprevir/sofosbuvir.

questions.model_answer: Test for the NS3 Q80K polymorphism. Q80K is present in about 40% of genotype 1a isolates and confers low-level resistance to simeprevir; it adversely affects response when simeprevir is used for short durations or in patients with cirrhosis, so if Q80K is detected an alternative regimen should be chosen.

cohort_answer.text: Check for Q80K polymorphism, confers low level resistance to in vitro simeprevir activity. If the patient is NON-CIRRHOTIC -> this does not matter. Can treat for 12 weeks. If the patient is CIRRHOTIC and Q80K polymorphism present, consider a different regimen. As a rule -> if patient has cirrhosis, we have to check for resistance. If the patient is not cirrhotic resistance testing is not usually needed.

questions.question: Hepatitis C virus.

parts.text: List 4 (or 6) clinical scenarios in which testing for HCV RNA (qualitative or quantitative) is indicated.
State the most important prognostic factor in the treatment of hepatitis C.
List 4 modes of transmission/acquisition of hepatitis C.

parts_raw.text: A. 4 (or 6) reasons (ie. Clinical scenarios) to test for Hep C RNA (either qualitative or quantitative)
Most important prognostic factor in treatment of Hep C
C. List 4 modes of transmission/acquisition.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Confirm active infection in an anti-HCV-positive patient (distinguish current infection from resolved/past infection). (2) Assess/confirm cure after treatment (SVR, i.e. undetectable RNA 12 weeks post-therapy). (3) Suspected acute infection or recent documented exposure (e.g. needlestick), where RNA becomes detectable before antibody seroconversion; RNA tested 2-4 weeks after exposure. (4) Immunosuppressed or dialysis patients in whom antibody may be falsely negative. (5) Perinatal evaluation of an infant born to an HCV-infected mother (maternal antibody unreliable). (6) Suspected reinfection after prior cure in an anti-HCV-positive person.
b) The single most important prognostic factor is the presence and stage of hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis (especially decompensated cirrhosis), which lowers SVR, restricts regimen choice/duration, and drives long-term outcomes; in the interferon era viral genotype was the dominant predictor.
c) (1) Parenteral/percutaneous exposure to blood (injection drug use, transfusion/blood products, needlestick). (2) Nosocomial/unsafe medical injection or procedure. (3) Vertical (maternal-infant) transmission. (4) Sexual transmission (notably HIV-positive MSM).
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific HCV RNA testing indications (part a) are established diagnostic practice (AASLD/IDSA, CASL); this slice supports RNA testing before antibody seroconversion and in postexposure workup but does not enumerate all scenarios.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Positive Ab - Active HCV infection (confirm diagnosis during clinical disease, post-exposure); Post-Treatment (look for response, sustained virologic response); Re-exposure after cure. Negative/Unreliable Ab - Vertical transmission (infant during first 18 months, serology unreliable due to maternal antibodies, use RNA instead); Immunosuppressed Patients (hemodialysis, transplant recipients, advanced HIV - high rate of false negative Ab, RNA should be done regardless of antibody results); Acute hepatitis or Recent exposure (if high clinical suspicion, perform RNA as it may be detectable prior to reactive antibodies; Ab takes 2-6 months after exposure to develop); Concern for transmissibility e.g. deceased donor organ transplantation or needle stick origin, need result quickly

Most important prognostic factor: Presence of cirrhosis - restricts certain drugs, predicts overall mortality and need for transplant, HCC only occurs in those with cirrhosis with Hep C (unlike Hep B)

C: Vertical transmission. Parenteral transmission (Blood transfusion, IVDU, needlestick). Nosocomial transmission (unsafe medical practices). Transplant. Sexual transmission

questions.question: Pegylated interferon in the treatment of hepatitis C.

parts.text: Explain the rationale for and benefits of pegylated interferon in hepatitis C therapy.
List 4 factors affecting response to treatment and prognosis.

parts_raw.text: A. The rationale for and benefits of pegylated interferon in Hep C therapy
List 4 factors affecting response to treatment and prognosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Rationale/benefits: pegylation (attaching polyethylene glycol) slows clearance and prolongs the interferon half-life, giving sustained plasma drug levels and allowing convenient once-weekly dosing. This produced higher SVR rates than standard (thrice-weekly) interferon-alpha, and higher still when PEG-interferon was combined with oral ribavirin. Note: in the current direct-acting antiviral (DAA) era, interferon-containing regimens are no longer recommended (neither AASLD nor IDSA recommend them).
b) (1) Viral genotype (genotype 1 and 4 least responsive to interferon; genotype 3 the standout in the DAA era). (2) Presence of cirrhosis, particularly decompensated. (3) Baseline HCV RNA (viral load). (4) Presence of resistance-associated substitutions (chiefly NS5A); host IL28B genotype and prior treatment experience are additional predictors.

cohort_answer.text:
A: No longer recommended for HCV infection

Factors: Adherence, Drug-drug interactions, Decompensated cirrhosis, Co-infection, Resistance

questions.question: Hepatitis C virus screening and treatment.

parts.text: List 4 populations in which to test for hepatitis C.
State the most common HCV genotype in Canada.
List 2 direct-acting antiviral regimens for hepatitis C.

parts_raw.text: Populations to test in (4)
Most common genotype in Canada
DAA regimens (2)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) All adults at least once (birth-cohort/universal one-time screening). (2) People who inject drugs (ongoing/past injection drug use). (3) Patients on maintenance hemodialysis and other immunosuppressed groups. (4) HIV-positive MSM / those on HIV PrEP, and long-term sexual partners of HCV-infected persons; also pregnant persons.
b) Genotype 1 (predominantly genotype 1a) is the most common genotype in Canada.
c) (1) Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks (pangenotypic; add ribavirin in decompensated cirrhosis). (2) Glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks if no cirrhosis, 12 weeks if compensated cirrhosis (pangenotypic).
questions.beyond_mandell: Screening populations (part a) and the Canadian genotype distribution (part b) come from CASL/CADTH/CTFPHC guidance; this Mandell slice grounds the DAA regimens (part c) but not the Canadian screening list or genotype epidemiology.

cohort_answer.text: Populations to test: All adults >18 at least one screening; Ongoing IVDU; MSM who have HIV or are on PrEP for HIV; Pregnant women; Long term sexual partners of individuals with HCV; Patients on maintenance hemodialysis. Most common genotype: Genotype 1. DAA regimens: Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks (+ribavirin if cirrhotic); Glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks

questions.model_answer: (1) Elbasvir-grazoprevir for 12 weeks (only if no elbasvir NS5A RAS detected on baseline testing in genotype 1a). (2) Glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks (no cirrhosis). (3) Ledipasvir-sofosbuvir for 12 weeks (the 8-week shortened option is NOT applicable here because baseline HCV RNA is 8 million IU/mL, above the 6 million IU/mL threshold). (4) Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: Regimens reflect AASLD/IDSA (Table 154.4) initial-treatment options for genotype 1a; Canadian (CASL) first-line recommendations align with these four.

cohort_answer.text: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa); Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Maviret); Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni); Elbasvir/grazoprevir (Zepatier).

questions.model_answer: Simeprevir - NS3/4A serine protease inhibitor (first-generation); approved for genotype 1 infection (used with an NS5B polymerase inhibitor such as sofosbuvir). cohort_answer.text: Simeprevir - NS3a/4a inhibitor - Genotype 1. Sofosbuvir - RNA polymerase inhibitor - Genotypes 1,2,3,4. Additional: NS5B=RNA dependent RNA polymerase, Polymerase inhibitors (Sofosbuvir, Dasabuvir); NS5A=Viral replication/assembly, NS5A inhibitors (Daclatasvir, Ledipasvir, Ombitasvir); NS3=Serine Protease, Protease inhibitors (Telaprevir, Boceprevir, Simeprevir, Paritaprevir).

questions.question: Name 6 different viruses that cause cancer and the type of cancer each causes.

parts.text: Name 6 different oncogenic viruses and the cancer each causes.

parts_raw.text: Name 6 different viruses that cause cancer and what type of cancer?

questions.model_answer: (1) HPV (high-risk 16/18) - cervical, anogenital and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. (2) Hepatitis B virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (3) Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (4) Epstein-Barr virus - Burkitt and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (and Hodgkin/post-transplant lymphoma). (5) HHV-8 (KSHV) - Kaposi sarcoma (and primary effusion lymphoma). (6) HTLV-1 - adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. (Merkel cell polyomavirus - Merkel cell carcinoma is an acceptable additional answer.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Only HPV is covered in this chapter; the other oncogenic viruses are from established virology (Mandell general/oncovirus chapters).
